core.p: **Part (b)**: Explain the importance of the supernatural **elsewhere in the novella**. In your answer you must consider: how the ghosts are presented; why Dickens uses them. You should refer to the context. (20 marks)

essays.q: Explain the importance of the supernatural elsewhere in the novella.
essays.t: Model essay: the Ghosts and their purpose
essays.text:
Dickens uses the Ghosts as an escalating moral education, moving from warning to memory to empathy to fear; because his Preface hopes the book will ‘haunt their houses pleasantly’, the Ghosts’ methods are also Dickens’s methods for changing his readers.

Marley’s ghost begins as Gothic horror, announced by the face in the door knocker and the sound of a chain dragged up the stairs, a familiar device in the popular Victorian tradition of telling ghost stories at Christmas. But his chain is symbolic: made of ‘cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and heavy purses’, it shows greed as self-imprisonment. ‘I wear the chain I forged in life… of my own free will’ stresses personal responsibility, and his wail that ‘Mankind was my business’ redefines a businessman’s duty. Marley is a warning: the fate that awaits Scrooge, and by implication the reader.

The Ghost of Christmas Past works through memory. Its paradoxical appearance, ‘like a child: yet not so like a child as like an old man’, captures the strange presence of the past in us, and its ‘bright clear jet of light’ represents truth. It rarely lectures; it simply shows Scrooge his lonely childhood and his lost love, Belle, and lets him feel. When Scrooge forces the extinguisher cap down on its light, Dickens shows how painful truth can be, and yet light still streams from beneath it.

The Ghost of Christmas Present is a ‘jolly Giant’ surrounded by food, a figure of abundance who invites Scrooge to ‘know me better’. He teaches empathy by showing the Cratchits and Tiny Tim, then turns social critic: he throws Scrooge’s ‘surplus population’ back at him and reveals Ignorance and Want, warning ‘beware this boy’. Here the supernatural becomes Dickens’s direct voice on the poverty of the ‘Hungry Forties’ and the dangers of neglecting children’s education.

The last Ghost is the most terrifying because it is silent. ‘Shrouded in a deep black garment’, with only an outstretched hand, it resembles the Grim Reaper, and its silence forces Scrooge to interpret the scenes himself: the unmourned death, the thieves, the Cratchits’ grief, and his own grave. Fear completes what memory and empathy began, and Scrooge vows to ‘live in the Past, the Present, and the Future’. The order of the Ghosts therefore mirrors the structure of a sermon or a moral fable, from warning to consequence. Dickens, as a novelist with a social purpose, uses the supernatural not to frighten for its own sake but to make readers see, feel and change, exactly as Scrooge does.
essays.thesis: Dickens uses the Ghosts as an escalating moral education, moving from warning to memory to empathy to fear, and because his Preface hopes the book will ‘haunt’ its readers, the Ghosts’ methods are also Dickens’s methods for changing his audience.
why: **AO1**: a clear concept (escalating education; ghosts as Dickens’s methods).
**AO3**: ghost-story tradition, Hungry Forties, education, purpose.
Each ghost’s method is analysed, not just described.

summary: A full grade 9 part (b) model essay on the Ghosts and their purpose, arguing that they form an escalating moral education that mirrors Dickens’s own aim of haunting his readers into change.

terms.d: Learning right from wrong through experience.
A genre using ghosts, darkness and dread.
